difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: a single concept (choosing the past perfect continuous before a simple-past 'when' clause) answered by direct recall, well within 1.5 minutes.
stem:
We __________ tennis in the lawn when it suddenly started to rain.

Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.

solution.quick: The clause *"when it suddenly started to rain"* is in the simple past, so the blank must describe an action that was **already in progress (for some time) at that past moment**. That is the past perfect continuous, *had been playing*. Answer: **(B)**.

steps.title: Locate the time reference
steps.body: The second clause, *"when it suddenly started to rain"*, uses the **simple past** (*started*). The whole sentence therefore narrates a **past** event, and the moment the rain began is the reference point.

steps.title: Decide what the blank must express
steps.body:
The playing was **already going on, and had been going on for a while**, when the rain interrupted it. An ongoing action that continued up to a moment in the past is expressed by the **past perfect continuous**:

$$
\text{had been} + \text{verb-}ing \;\Rightarrow\; \text{had been playing}
$$

(The past continuous *were playing* would also fit, but it is not offered.)

steps.title: Eliminate the other forms
steps.body:
- **(A) have been playing** is the *present* perfect continuous. It links an activity to the **present moment** (*We have been playing for an hour*) and cannot be anchored to a finished past event such as *started to rain*.
- **(C) would have been playing** is a conditional (hypothetical) form, used for unreal situations: *If it hadn't rained, we would have been playing*. The sentence states a fact and has no condition.
- **(D) could be playing** expresses a present or future **possibility**. Both the modality and the time frame are wrong for a completed past event.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: *We **had been playing** tennis in the lawn when it suddenly started to rain.* The answer is **(B)**.

solution.teaching:
**Timeline thinking for tenses.** Every tense places an action relative to a reference time. In a narrative about the past, the reference time is the past event described in the simple past (here, *it started to rain*).

**The forms involved:**

| Form | Structure | Reference point | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Present perfect continuous | *have/has been + V-ing* | **now** | activity from the past up to now: *I have been studying since 8.* |
| Past continuous | *was/were + V-ing* | a past moment | action in progress at a past moment: *We were playing when it rained.* |
| Past perfect continuous | *had been + V-ing* | a past moment | action that had been going on **for some time up to** a past moment: *We had been playing for an hour when it rained.* |
| Perfect conditional continuous | *would have been + V-ing* | hypothetical | unreal past: *If it hadn't rained, we would have been playing.* |
| Modal + continuous | *could be + V-ing* | now/future | possibility: *They could be playing now.* |

**The interruption pattern.** *"[longer action] **when** [short past event]"* is a classic structure. The short event is in the simple past, and the longer, ongoing action takes a past continuous form: *was/were V-ing*, or *had been V-ing* when you want to stress that it had already been going on for a while.

**Why the present perfect fails.** The present perfect always has one foot in the present. *"We have been playing … when it started to rain"* mixes a present-anchored form with a finished past event, which is a sequence-of-tense error.

**Back to this question.** The rain began at a definite past moment, and the playing was in progress before and up to that moment. Among the options, only *had been playing* is a non-modal past form, so (B) is correct.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: *Have been playing* (present perfect continuous) is anchored to the present moment, but the reference event *started to rain* is in the past. The tenses do not agree.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: *Had been playing* (past perfect continuous) describes an action that was in progress up to a moment in the past. This is exactly the situation of play interrupted by rain.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: *Would have been playing* is a hypothetical (conditional) form that needs an unreal condition, e.g. *if it had not rained*. The sentence reports an actual event.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: *Could be playing* expresses a present or future possibility. It fits neither the past time frame nor the factual meaning of the sentence.

solution.shortcut: Look at the verb in the other clause: *started* is simple past, so the blank needs a **past** form. (A) is present-anchored and (C) and (D) are modal (hypothetical or possibility) forms, which leaves only (B).
solution.commonTrap: Choosing (A) because *have been playing* sounds natural for an ongoing activity, without noticing that the reference event (*started to rain*) is in the past. Some students also pick (C) because the longer form sounds more formal.
